stance_basis: letter and attached comments call for ORV use to be presumed detrimental and prohibited on all public lands unless proven otherwise, with extensive specific objections to the draft EIS
summary: Michael McCloskey, as Executive Director of the Sierra Club, submitted a formal comment letter with detailed attached comments opposing the draft EIS for ORV implementation of Executive Order 11644. The Sierra Club argued that ORV use should be presumed harmful and all public lands closed to ORVs by default, opened only after study proves acceptable impact, and raised numerous specific objections to the draft's language, criteria, and emphasis on user-group benefits over resource protection.
complaint_summary: The Sierra Club's attached comments argue that ORV use should be presumed detrimental and all public lands closed to ORVs by default, criticize the draft EIS for prioritizing user-group interests over resource protection, and provide extensive page-by-page objections covering licensing, carrying capacity, wildlife impacts, desert erosion, snowmobile damage, noise, and the need for objective criteria for area designations.

statement.text:
Sierra Club Comments on the
Draft Environmental Impact Statement
For Department of Interior Implementation Of
Presidential Order 11644
Concerning the Use of Off Road Vehicles on Public Lands
General Comments
(1) ORV areas should be located near urban areas where possible and not allowed in more remote lands of a wilderness or semi-wilderness character. Most ORV users are interested in testing their machines and not in access to scenic areas. These areas, however, should not be immediately adjacent to homes where a citizen's right to privacy, peace, and quiet would be threatened. ORV areas distant from urban areas would create traffic congestion with accompanying air pollution. Control would be easier to maintain closer to urban centers.
(2) No mention is made of the amount of land that will be closed to ORV vs. that which will be open. This will probably turn out to be the most critical issue when the program is implemented. The statement should recognize this problem and state that the interests of all of the people will be placed above those of the ORV operators when those interests are in conflict. The primary charge of public land administrators is to protect resources first and to accommodate various users of the land second.
(3) Since our public lands are not limitless, regulation beyond the zoning emphasized in the statement will be needed. If ORV areas are over-used and are receiving unacceptable damage, the solution should not be to open up more areas to their use. Consideration must be given to rationing their use. This could be done by issuing permits to individual ORV operators and restricting the frequency of their use. This is being considered for wilderness areas now and there is no reason why other users of public lands should not be similarly restricted. Before any ORV area is opened up an attempt to determine its carrying capacity should be made in order to limit damage. The carrying capacity should not be

exceeded under any circumstance.
Specific Comments
<u>Page 5, b-i.</u> The Sierra Club strongly supports the statement requiring operators of ORVs to be licensed. Since a lot of ORV damage to the environment is caused by unsupervised, under age operators, strong regulations regarding under age operators must be made and enforced. The adult supervisor should be held legally responsible for any damage caused by under age operators under his supervision.
<u>b-i (d)</u>. <u>Excessive</u> damage should be changed to something like <u>permanent</u> and noticeable damage. Damage by ORV should be controlled far short of being excessive.
<u>b-iii</u>. The Sierra Club strongly supports this good provision requiring proper muffler and spark arrestor equipment on all vehicles and that this equipment be in good working order and in constant operation.
<u>Page 6 (iv)</u>. Organized off road vehicle events must not be allowed <u>under any</u> <u>circumstance</u> in any areas normally closed to ORVs. Bonds must be put up by people conducting such events. Provision must also be made to rehabilitate and restore areas impacted by these events.
Page 10, lines 10-11. This states that lands will remain open to public use unless closed for a specific reason. This should not apply to ORVs because of their unquestioned damage. All BLM lands should be closed to ORV and then opened up on a parcel by parcel basis after a study has been shown that the leval of ORV damage will be acceptable. This should be true of all federally owned land, not just BLM land.
Page 11, lines 1-5. The terms used to identify ORV areas are qualitative.

Objective criteria are needed or at least a system for arriving at objective criteria. If the decision to open or close an area becomes merely subjective, then we can expect decisions to be made only on the basis of pressure and not on what is best to protect the resources. Furthermore, determination of ORV carrying capacity must be made for all areas open for their use and limited to such levels as the environment can handle without significant environmental damage.

Page 12, lines 8-11. ORVs do cause damage in most areas with substantial use. Repeated use by large numbers (in excess of the carrying capacity) causes excessive damage in nearly all types of terrain and vegetation.
Furthermore, ORVs are not primarily used for access to remote areas when all use is considered collectively. Very few ORV operators are interested in access as much as they are in testing out their machine. ORVs are used for sport and not for an appreciation of the aesthetic and cultural qualities of the public lands. If ORVs were used merely for access we would have minimal conflict with them.
Page 13, line 1. Emphasis is placed upon the benefits to user groups. This statement should acknowledge that the public lands belong to everyone, not just user groups. The public lands of the nation need to be managed so that the resources are managed in the best interests of all the people -- present and future generations -- and not just for the user groups who happen to be on the scene at this point in time.
<u>Page 13</u>. The discussion of soil erosion in the last paragraph should include wind erosion of desert soils. Under normal conditions much of the desert surface is covered by desert pavement — a covering of pebble to boulder size rocks, the smaller material having been carried away by wind erosion. ORV wheels break up this thin crust exposing the finer soil beneath to further wind erosion. The problem is especially severe where cross country races are held in the desert. Participants take off in waves, sometimes one-mile-across lines, axle to axle, cutting a huge swath of destruction across the desert.
Page 14, paragraph 2. Snowmobiles do more than create a litter problem.

Studies are increasingly demonstrating significant environmental impact on vegetation from snowmobiles as the result of twig breakage and snow compaction. Also, the snowmobile is used as a vehicle to chase a number of species of wildlife, which all too frequently causes severe exhaustion and sometimes death. Harassment

129
of wildlife of any sort must not be allowed.
Page 14, last paragraph. The dust problem is especially bad in the desert and should be mentioned in this statement.
Page 15, last paragraph. The California Department of Fish and Game has set up quali guzzlers in many areas of the California desert and some game birds are entirely dependent on this source of water. Cross country motorcycle races have been routed right by some of these. Vandalism in areas accessible only by ORVs has also been a critical problem with quali guzzlers.
The Desert Bighorn Sheep is known to disappear in areas of heavy human use.

This species should receive a higher priority in management decisions than ORVs.
Page 16, paragraph 2. It should be emphasized here that ORV use should be considered harmful to wildlife until proven otherwise. All areas should be considered closed until it is shown that ORVs would have an acceptable impact upon wildlife.
Page 16, paragraph 3. The only ORV users who might need access to game management purposes are the game and land managers themselves. If it is determined that an area should be closed to ORVs, then hunters should walk or ride horses. It should be very clear that an area normally closed to ORVs will not be opened to hunters on ORVs merely because of a surplus of game.
Page 17, line 11. This mentions revenues from sales of motorcycles. It should be recognized that not all motorcycles are used as ORVs. Only those that are used as ORVs should be included in the statement.
Page 17, lines 15-16. Winter access to small towns via snowmobiles can be on snow covered roads and need not be cross country.
Page 18, line 11. The case for strengthened family relationships caused by ORV use should be proven. Saying there is reason to believe this is true is not enough. The reasons should be spelled out.

Page 19, last paragraph. The signs of ORV use are very offensive to non-users. This remark should remain in the statement and receive more emphasis.
Page 21, paragraph 2. It is true implementation will be costly. The statement should place more emphasis upon this fact and groups like the Sierra Club can help in acquiring the necessary funds to effectively control ORVs.
Page 22, line 6. This recognizes a land ethic itself. This is very important and should be greatly emphasized by the use of a separate heading and a greatly expanded text.
This same paragraph again only refers to users of public lands and does not mention that all of the people own the public lands. Their best interests need to be considered.
Page 24, line 10. Urban dwellers will be especially resentful if ORV areas are established within hearing range of homes.
Page 26, lines 6-8. This sentence implies that decisions will be semi-permanent. If ORV areas are shown to suffer unacceptable damage they should be closed. It should not be implied that any ORV area will not be closed at a future date if necessary.
Page 26, lines 9-12. The problems mentioned in this paragraph would be minimized if all areas were considered closed and then opened to ORVs only after a careful study shows damage would be acceptable.
Page 29, line 4. "Inspiration" is hardly the word to use when discussing the benefits of ORV benefits. It should be deleted.
